v: Bio Lab One has water. That is one valve, by hand, on the oldest run on the base. Everything after this is the same job with more of it happening at once.
Open the loop: push FLOW into the OPEN band.

With the valve shut the markers moved but stayed where they were. That motion is temperature. Now they are travelling along the pipe, and that is flow. A pipe that is full and a pipe that is flowing are two different states.
Compare the markers at the wall with the markers down the middle.

They are not moving at the same speed. Friction between the fluid and the pipe surface holds the fluid at the wall almost stationary; further from the wall less of that drag reaches it. The yellow curve is that spread of speed across the bore: the velocity profile.
Close FLOW down into the TRICKLE band.

At this speed the fluid travels in parallel layers that do not mix, and the profile becomes a long parabola with the centre at about twice the average speed. This is laminar flow. REYNOLDS, the number that identifies it, is now below 2,300.
Leave FLOW alone. Push TEMPERATURE into the HOT band.

The valve has not moved, so the fluid is travelling at the same speed. Heating water lowers its viscosity. Reynolds is velocity x bore / viscosity, so lower viscosity means higher Reynolds. Above 4,000 the layers break up and mix: turbulent flow, and the profile goes blunt.
Switch the loop to LIQUID PROPANE.

Nothing else changed and DELIVERED went up. Flow through a fixed restriction is q = Cv x sqrt(dP / SG). Propane has a specific gravity of 0.501 — half of water — so more of it passes for the same pressure drop. Its viscosity is five times lower too, which is why REYNOLDS jumped.
Now use it. Deliver 0.50 gpm and keep the flow laminar.

That is the chain, used. Propane could not do it at any temperature — too little viscosity, so Reynolds is always high. Water could not either until you cooled it, because cold water is more viscous. Fluid, temperature and valve position together decide what a line does.
COMMS: And there it is in a real line — centre running away from the wall, exactly like the loop. You will see it in every pipe on this base now that you know to look for it.

COMMS: There it is. And look at what that gauge did — it sat at nothing while the line behind the valve was already full and already under pressure. Pressure is not flow. The wheel did not make water. It gave what was already standing there somewhere to go.

COMMS: Nothing down this end is automated. No actuators, no remote, no screens. Every run in Four-B gets opened by somebody standing where you are, reading a gauge with their own eyes.The engineer you stood in for today walked this round for six years.
COMMS: Bio Lab One has water. Nobody up there will think about you again until it stops — that is the job.Play your cards right, you might make a decent one yourself.
Open the MAIN SUPPLY valve. Drag the hand wheel.

60 psig at the manifold — and nothing is moving. In Four-B the gauge sat downstream, so it only woke up once water ran. This one sits on the manifold: the line is loaded and perfectly still, with every bed shut.

The valve created nothing — it opened a path, and the pressure spent itself. And watch what left first: that run was new pipe, full of air, which had to vent out the emitters before water reached a single root.
Open BED 2. Keep an eye on Bed 1’s number.
Bed 1 dropped when Bed 2 opened, and nobody touched Bed 1. One supply, two demands — what divides at the tee is all there ever was.

Bed 3 is on the old run with a reducer in it. Same valve, same manifold pressure, noticeably less flow — and watch the particles sprint through that throat. Squeeze the bore and velocity goes up while pressure goes down. The restriction is in the pipe, not the valve.
Now throttle BED 1 back to about a quarter open — and watch Bed 3.
Bed 3 came up and nobody touched Bed 3. Add resistance to one branch and manifold pressure rises for every other branch. In a shared system there is no local change.
Last job: balance the bay. Three identical beds should drink about the same — get all three within a tenth of a gallon of each other.

That is commissioning. You balanced down to the weakest branch: Bed 3 can never pass more than its reducer allows, so the other two came back to meet it. The whole bay now runs at Bed 3’s ceiling — that reducer is not costing one bed, it is capping all three.
Bay 3 is commissioned. Three beds balanced, and a reducer in line 3 that is now holding the whole bay back.
Isolate line 3 — shut BED 3 right off.

You do not cut into a live line. And look what isolating it did to everyone else: shut one demand and manifold pressure climbs for every branch left open. Same rule as commissioning, now with a spanner in your hand.
Now take the reducer out. Click the fitting.
Coupler and a new spool, same bore as the rest of the branch. And line 3 is full of air again — you just had it open to the bay. That will have to vent before water reaches the roots.
Balance the bay first — all three even, and as high as Bed 3 will let them go.
Open BED 3 back up and bring the whole bay wide open.
Open BED 3 back up and bring the whole bay wide open.
Line 3 is a line again.

Line 3 is a line again. The repair is sound — but nobody wrote down what the bay was doing before you touched it, and that number only ever existed in the bay you did not stop to read.

A repair you cannot measure is a repair you cannot defend.
COMMS: Before you start — your call on the order. We can balance the bay the way it stands and write the numbers down, then pull the reducer. Or we can just pull it now and balance once, afterwards.
